title: The magazine predicted electronic record-handling by 1990.
description:
Xerox PARC. Told Business Week he didn't know how much paper he'd still want; not the 'paperless by 1990' claim usually attributed to him.

The magazine predicted electronic record-handling by 1990. A separate claim from Pake's own hedge about a desk terminal by 1995; the two get merged in almost every retelling.

US business paper use nearly doubled in three years. 850 billion pages in 1981 to 1.4 trillion by 1984, as photocopiers and early computers multiplied documents instead of replacing them.

Office paper use rose again once email arrived. US office paper consumption grew more than 14% between 1995 and 2000.

Paper use only started falling once everyone had a phone.

Sources:
- https://www.csmonitor.com/2005/1212/p13s01-wmgn.html - established the exact 1975 Business Week article ('The Office of the Future', 30 June 1975), its 'most record-handling will be electronic' claim pegged to 1990, and the verbatim George Pake quote and his own, separate 1995 estimate.
- https://expexinc.com/in-1975-business-week-prophesized-that-the-office-of-the-future-would-be-a-paperless-one/ - independently corroborated the same Pake quote and its attribution to Xerox PARC's June 1975 Business Week feature.
- https://cool.culturalheritage.org/byorg/abbey/ap/ap02/ap02-3/ap02-309.html - established that US business paper use rose from 850 billion to 1.4 trillion pages between 1981 and 1984, citing historian Edward Tenner.
- https://www.sdcexec.com/sourcing-procurement/manufacturing/article/10290027/paper-still-the-net-best-thing - established, via Sellen & Harper's 'The Myth of the Paperless Office' (2001), that US office paper consumption rose more than 14% between 1995 and 2000.
- https://www.afandpa.org/news/2024/afpa-details-us-paper-production-and-capacity-trends - established that US printing-writing paper capacity peaked around 2000 and had fallen to about 12% of total capacity, under 10 million tons, by 2023.
